title: Dice Roll
primary_metric: total in-person compliance-monitoring program cost (mileage, lodging, meals and incidentals, and staff time) for the same 5-county visit plan, The Statewide Draw vs. The Front Range Loop

options.A: The Statewide Draw -- a two-stage (multistage) sample: 5 of 12 working-roster counties chosen by simple random sampling, then audit sessions inside each selected county chosen by systematic sampling, so every region of the state has a real chance of an in-person Division visit
options.B: The Front Range Loop -- a convenience sample of the 5 counties nearest the Denver office, cheaper and simpler to run, but the Eastern Plains, the San Luis Valley, and the Western Slope are never visited, no matter how many cycles pass

new_coverage_note: No skill claimed here has n==0 in readmodel/standards_spine.json, so case-write's mechanical new_coverage check (which requires new_coverage[] entries to have n==0) is correctly empty. This case's real reason to exist is reinforcement of the thinnest corner of Sampling And Experiments: Multistage Sampling remains a genuine n=1 singleton at authoring time (its only existing coverage is 'Movie Executive' -- cases/full-reach also targets it but was researched, not published, this session, so it has not yet moved spine n) -- a single point of failure in the coverage matrix -- and Cluster Sampling, Systematic Sampling, and Convenience Sampling are all thin at n=2. This case brings Multistage to n=2 (or n=3 once full-reach also publishes) and the other three to n=3 (or n=4), and every one is genuinely forced by a Challenge-3 deliverable (see LEARNING_GOALS.md's forces-test), not padded. Same reinforcement-carve-out pattern as cases/full-reach (see skills/case-publish/SKILL.md's new_coverage[] exception for legacy_conversion_note/reinforcement_note cases).
reinforcement_note: Targets the singleton Multistage Sampling (n=1) and the thin n=2 skills Cluster Sampling, Systematic Sampling, and Convenience Sampling in Statistics And Probability > Sampling And Experiments, per readmodel/standards_spine.json as of authoring (2026-09-09). This case is a deliberately distinct real-world grounding of the same thin skill cluster full-reach (a food-safety supply-chain setting) also targets this session: same four sampling-method skills, different real setting (Colorado state election-audit compliance monitoring, C.R.S. Sec. 1-7-515), different protagonist, different real sourced data, different cost model and margin. Reinforcing a genuine singleton and three n=2 skills from two independent real-world angles in the same session is intentional per the project owner's direct request to ground this concept in a government/politics setting as well as an industry setting.

protagonist: Marisol Ibarra, Compliance Audit Coordinator, Colorado Department of State Elections Division -- a former county poll worker, unflappable under scrutiny, who keeps a six-sided die on her desk from the training where an instructor first used dice to teach random sampling

deliverables.text: A population-and-sample description: how many counties are on the case's 12-county working roster, how many the state actually has, the size of this cycle's visit sample, and what percent of the working roster -- and separately what percent of the full state -- that sample represents.

A Statewide Draw sampling plan: the realized simple-random first-stage county draw, and for each selected county the systematic-sampling interval and starting point used to choose which scheduled audit sessions to observe.

A cluster-sampling cost check: the review-time cost of observing every scheduled audit session (not a systematic subsample) at the 5 Statewide Draw counties, showing why the plan systematically subsamples sessions inside each selected county instead of observing the whole cluster.

A Front Range Loop representativeness analysis: which counties sit inside vs. permanently outside its reach, plus a selection-probability comparison for a specific Western Slope/San Luis Valley county in a single cycle and across three consecutive cycles under each option.
A total program cost comparison (mileage, lodging, meals and incidentals, and staff time) for The Statewide Draw vs. The Front Range Loop.

Two original visual displays: a bar graph of each option's total program cost by category, and a pie chart of what share of Colorado's population lives in the Front Range Loop's 5 reachable counties versus the rest of the state.

appendices.title: How To… Math Questions To Research

balance.argument_a: The Statewide Draw gives all 12 roster counties -- Front Range, plains, valley, and Western Slope alike -- a real, calculable inclusion probability (5/12 per cycle, about 41.7%) for an in-person Division visit, and makes it likely (about 80%) that any specific remote county lands a visit at least once across three consecutive election cycles. The Front Range Loop gives the state's Eastern Plains, San Luis Valley, and Western Slope counties a permanent, structural 0% chance -- not a probability, a guarantee of exclusion, no matter how many cycles run or how the travel budget is spent.
balance.argument_b: The Front Range Loop reaches the same 5 counties at a total program cost of $2,920.48 -- $330.48 mileage plus $0.00 lodging plus the same $340.00 M&IE and $2,250.00 staff time every option pays -- versus The Statewide Draw's $3,624.64 ($814.64 mileage, $220.00 lodging for the 2 overnight counties, Kit Carson and Alamosa). That is $704.16 less, a 19.43% saving, because all 5 Front Range Loop counties are inside a same-day, no-overnight driving radius of the Denver office, so it pays $0 of the $220.00 lodging line A carries.
balance.margin_basis: Compare total program cost (mileage + lodging + meals and incidentals + compliance-monitor staff time, at 5 visits under each option) for Option A vs. Option B using Appendix C's rates and Appendix A's distances.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: One-way distance beyond which an overnight stay is required
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public Division policy fixes an exact same-day-versus-overnight cutoff for this monitoring program. 150 miles one-way is roughly a 2.5-hour drive each way -- beyond that, a round trip plus a real working stretch of time inside the audit session no longer fits a single business day.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The answer is sensitive to this value.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Loaded daily cost of a compliance monitor's travel day
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public figure exists for the Division's specific internal cost-accounting rate for a monitoring day. Set consistent with a Colorado state classified analyst's salary band loaded with standard public-sector benefits and overhead, prorated to a single workday. Applied identically to every visit under both options.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The answer is sensitive to this value -- it is the case's single most load-bearing assumption (see sensitivity_model.py FLEX).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Number of site visits this cycle
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public figure exists for the Division's exact travel/staff-day budget for in-person compliance monitoring; the case fixes a small number consistent with a compact state elections-oversight staff.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Applies identically to both options -- does not by itself favor either one.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: This case's 12-county working roster stands in for Colorado's full 64-county population
modeling_assumptions.basis: Modeling every one of the state's 64 counties would make the dataset unworkable for a classroom exercise; the 12-county roster spans all of the state's recognized geographic regions, preserving the real geographic spread that drives the tradeoff.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Does not affect the cost margin; affects only the scale of the D1 population-and-sample arithmetic.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Per-session review and documentation cost, if a session is observed
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public figure exists for the Division's internal cost of writing up and filing a single observed-session report. Set at a modest, round figure consistent with a short compliance write-up. Used only in Challenge D3's illustrative full-cluster-census cost check.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Does not affect the primary A-vs-B cost margin (Challenge D5), which never includes this figure; only affects D3's own separate comparison.

sensitivity_note: SPEC §6: the A-vs-B cost margin (19.43%) is sensitive to MA2's loaded daily staff-cost assumption and, to a lesser degree, MA1's overnight-distance threshold -- see sensitivity_model.py FLEX = ["staff_daily_rate", "overnight_threshold_mi"]. mileage_rate ($0.68/mi, S7) is deliberately excluded from FLEX -- it is a cited state rate, not a stated assumption; P6 (data decay), not P5, is the right probe for it. A -50% perturbation on staff_daily_rate alone pushes the margin to 28.17%, over the 20% cap; a +50% perturbation brings it to 14.83%. A +50%/-50% perturbation on the overnight threshold moves it to 16.91%/21.80% respectively. The representativeness argument for A (selection probability reaching every region) does not depend on either assumption and is unaffected by this sensitivity.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA2's $450/day loaded compliance-monitor cost has no public Division cost-accounting figure; it is a documented good-faith estimate built from the closest public analogue (a Colorado state classified-analyst salary band, loaded with standard public-sector benefits and overhead, prorated to a workday). A -50% swing on this single estimate alone pushes the margin to 28.17%, over the SPEC §2 20% cap -- disclosed here, in Appendix D's MA2 row, and in the FACILITATOR.md sensitivity note and Q1/Q4, not eliminated.

MA1's 150-mile one-way overnight cutoff has no public Division policy behind it; it is a documented good-faith estimate (roughly a 2.5-hour drive each way, the point past which a round trip plus a working stretch inside the audit session no longer fits a single business day). A -50% swing pushes the margin to 21.80%, just over the 20% cap -- disclosed here and in the FACILITATOR.md sensitivity note and Q4, not eliminated.

catalog.ask: Election officials have to inspect five counties out of dozens -- and how those five get chosen could decide whether the whole audit holds up under legal challenge. The cheap way to pick them looks almost identical to the defensible way. Almost.
